newsitem.title: INDIA: India allows foreign investment in government debt.
newsitem.headline: India allows foreign investment in government debt.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the country's market regulator, on Thursday announced foreign institutions will be allowed to invest in Indian government securities for the first time.

The move to open up the government debt market to foreigners was announced by the bourse watchdog along with a swathe of new rules governing share dealings, including fresh regulations related to takeovers.
SEBI said in a statement foreign institutional investors (FIIs) purchase of government securities would be subject to a cap within India's annual overall external commercial borrowing limit.
It also said proprietary funds belonging to FIIs would be allowed to invest in India's government debt market provided they are registered with their home tax authorities and regulators.
SEBI said a takeover offer, for a minimum additional 20 percent of a stock, would become mandatory as soon as a shareholder's holding crossed ten percent.
It allowed shareholders who held more than 10 percent but less than 51 percent of a stock to make "creeping acquisitions" of two percent in any 12-month period.
Any purchase by a person holding more than 51 percent would have to be made in a transparent manner, by a public tender offer, SEBI added.
It also said it had approved a stock lending scheme.

Under the scheme lenders will deposit securities with an approved intermediary who must have a minimum net worth of 500 million rupees ( $14.0 million) for a specified period, SEBI said in a statement.
The lender of shares will receive interest for the service and will continue to enjoy dividends and other rights on the shares, SEBI said.
To increase market transparency SEBI introduced a new rule to identify traders net exposure in any one stock, which could help deter overspeculative position-taking.
Brokers will have to declare their net long position in each stock, SEBI said. Stock exchanges already require brokers to disclose their net short position.
SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta told a news conference three foreign debt funds worth $253 million had been approved,
The three funds are J. Henry Schroeder, Credit-Suisse and Chescor, SEBI senior executive director Pratip Kar said.
